prompt: The bookshop's two copies each keep the session table in their own memory, behind Nginx's round-robin upstream. Shoppers are signed out at random, halfway through a basket. What is happening, and where do the two courses send the table?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 7; Web Servers and Caching, lesson 2.

choices.text: The cookie has no `Domain` attribute, so the browser keeps it from the second copy's port.
choices.why: The browser only talks to Nginx, at one name and one port, and its cookie reaches whichever copy Nginx picks.

choices.text: Round robin is the defect, and `hash $remote_addr` fixes it for good: each visitor always meets their own copy.
choices.why: Affinity is a workaround: an office behind one address lands on one copy, and a copy that stops takes its sessions with it.

choices.text: Half the requests reach a copy that never saw that session; keep the table in Redis, which both reach.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: `SameSite=Lax` drops the cookie from the requests Nginx forwards, so the copy behind it sees nobody signed in.
choices.why: `SameSite` is about which site caused the request; a proxy passing the `Cookie` header on is not another site.

prompt: To save processor time, a teammate wants to swap the Nginx in front of the bookshop for a load balancer that reads only up to layer 4. Today Nginx serves the files in `/var/www/ipe` itself and sends `location /api/` to the two copies of the shop. What would the swap lose?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 5; Web Servers and Caching, lesson 2.

choices.text: The split by path: such a box sees a connection to port 443 and none of the URL inside, so `/api/` looks like `/css/`.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Nothing in the routing: a layer 4 box still reads the path of every request, so only the choice of site by `Host` would be lost.
choices.why: Layer 4 stops at the port; the path is inside the request, which such a box never reads.

choices.text: Only the compression, since gzip belongs to layer 6 and the box works below it.
choices.why: Compression would go, and so would the split by path, which is what sends `/api/` to the shop.

choices.text: Nothing, if the box is given the certificate: holding it is what lets layer 4 read paths.
choices.why: Decrypting and reading the request, certificate in hand, is what a layer 7 balancer does.

prompt: The shop's wildcard certificate, `*.ipelivros.example`, is renewed by a DNS-01 plugin holding API credentials for the old DNS provider. Last month the domain's `NS` records were pointed at a new provider. Renewal now fails, although the plugin logs that it created the `_acme-challenge` TXT record. Why?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 8; Web Servers and Caching, lesson 3.

choices.text: DNS-01 is checked over port 80, and the redirect to HTTPS now swallows the request.
choices.why: That is HTTP-01; DNS-01 is checked in DNS, which is why it works for a machine nobody can reach.

choices.text: A wildcard cannot come from DNS-01, so every subdomain needs an HTTP-01 token of its own.
choices.why: It is the other way round: DNS-01 is the only challenge that can issue a wildcard.

choices.text: The new TXT record is still propagating, and it can take forty-eight hours to reach the CA.
choices.why: Nothing propagates, and no TTL helps a record held by servers nobody asks any more.

choices.text: It landed on servers nobody asks any more; the CA asks the ones `NS` names now.
choices.why: Right.

prompt: On the lab server, `sudo ss -ltn` lists `0.0.0.0:443`, `0.0.0.0:80`, `127.0.0.1:14000` and `127.0.0.1:8001`, among others, and no firewall is on. A colleague's laptop on the same network tries each of them. Which can it reach? Choose all that apply.
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 4; Web Servers and Caching, lesson 4.

choices.why: Loopback never reaches a network card: only the machine itself can ask, which is why the shop is reached through Nginx.
`0.0.0.0` is every address the machine has, the one on the office network included.

choices.text: Pebble's ACME API, on `127.0.0.1:14000`
choices.why: `127.0.0.1` is the machine talking to itself; nothing outside it can connect there.
Right: listening on every address, so the laptop's request on port 80 arrives.

prompt: On the handshake clock of the fundamentals course, a browser and a server are 150 milliseconds apart each way. The servers course says that without `keepalive` in the upstream, Nginx pays that same handshake before every request it passes to the application. On that clock, how many milliseconds pass between the SYN leaving and the request itself leaving with the ACK?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 2; Web Servers and Caching, lesson 2.

prompt: Readers in Lisbon say the bookshop, served from São Paulo, takes over a second to show its first page, and most of that second is round trips. The owner proposes doubling the server's bandwidth. What do the two courses say?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 3; Web Servers and Caching, lesson 7.

choices.text: It halves the wait, because each round trip then carries twice as many bytes at once.
choices.why: A wider pipe moves more side by side; nothing arrives sooner, and these round trips carry almost nothing.

choices.text: It leaves the slow part alone: the ocean sets each round trip, and an edge in Lisbon removes the crossing for cacheable files.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Turn on `gzip_types` instead: a third of the bytes is a third of the wait.
choices.why: Compression shrinks the transfer, the part that was already short; the round trips stay as long as the distance makes them.

choices.text: Put a CDN in front, and the signed-in basket speeds up exactly as much as the stylesheet does.
choices.why: A personal page must not be stored at the edge, so its request still crosses the ocean to the origin.

prompt: The shop starts reporting failures as `200 OK` with `{"error": "database unavailable"}` in the body, under its usual `Cache-Control: public, max-age=60`. Nginx caches `/api/` with `proxy_cache_use_stale error timeout http_500 http_502 http_503 http_504`. What goes wrong? Choose all that apply.
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 6; Web Servers and Caching, lesson 6.

choices.text: Nginx turns the answer into a `502`, because the body contradicts the status line.
choices.why: `502` means the application sent something that is not HTTP; a well-formed `200` passes, whatever its body says.

choices.text: The error is stored like any other answer and handed to every visitor for the next minute.
choices.why: Right: a cache files the failure under the address, because the number said it worked.

choices.text: The good copy from before the outage is never used, since Nginx sees a success and none of the listed failures.
choices.why: Right: the stale copy is a fallback for errors, and every one it knows of is a status code.

choices.text: `X-Cache-Status` reports `STALE`, so the failure at least shows in the headers.
choices.why: `STALE` means an expired copy was served instead of an error; here Nginx got a fresh success and stored it, `MISS` and then `HIT`.

prompt: Inside `location /api/`, a first proxy is written `proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8001/;`, with a slash after the port. A browser asks for `/api/books/3`, and the shop receives the path `___`.
hint: Web Servers and Caching, lesson 2.

A month later `promo.ipelivros.example`, run by an agency on plain HTTP, will not open for anybody who had visited the shop. What did lesson 4 advise?
hint: Web Servers and Caching, lesson 4.

choices.text: Nothing in advance: removing the header now clears the rule on each browser's next visit.
choices.why: Once a browser has seen the header, nothing changed on the server removes it before `max-age` runs out.

choices.text: Sending the header on the port-80 redirect as well, so that browsers learn the rule before they ever reach HTTPS.
choices.why: A browser ignores HSTS received over plain HTTP, because anybody on the path could have added it.

choices.text: Start at an hour, lengthen it once the certificate renews itself, and add subdomains once all are on HTTPS.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Nothing: `includeSubDomains` reaches only the names that the same Nginx serves.
choices.why: It covers every name under this one, including those another team runs somewhere else.

prompt: Asked straight, without the cache, every request to the shop waits 120 ms for its query, and lesson 5 puts the ceiling for ten at a time at about 80 requests a second. By the same reasoning, what is the ceiling, in requests a second, with 30 requests in flight, each still waiting 120 ms?
hint: Web Servers and Caching, lesson 5; Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 1.

prompt: The owner lowers a price and purges the copy, and the cache still ends up holding the old price for a whole lifetime. Put the events of lesson 6's race in the order they happened.
hint: Web Servers and Caching, lesson 6.
items: A visitor's request misses the cache
That request reads 8,990 from the database
The owner's update writes 7,990 to the database
The update purges the copy, which is not there yet
The slow request stores 8,990, fresh for another sixty seconds
trap: The tempting order puts the purge last, as the fix it was meant to be; it landed before the slow read stored its copy, which is why it removed nothing.

prompt: The bookshop goes behind a commercial CDN, set to reach the origin over plain HTTP because that was the quickest option to switch on. Visitors still see a valid padlock. What does that padlock describe?
hint: Web Servers and Caching, lesson 7; Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 9.

choices.text: Only the hop to the edge; the hop to the origin crosses a network in the clear.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The whole path, because the edge reuses the visitor's encrypted connection on its way to the origin.
choices.why: The edge ends the visitor's connection and opens a second one, which in this setting is plain.

choices.text: The whole path, as long as the origin listens only on `127.0.0.1`, as the lab's did.
choices.why: The lab's edge and origin shared one machine; a real origin is reached across networks the CDN does not own.

choices.text: The edge and the origin alike, since the CDN obtained the domain's certificate through ACME.
choices.why: Who obtained the certificate says nothing of the second hop; the padlock describes the hop the browser made.

prompt: The shop moves its session rows, the table behind the cookie, into the Redis that caches book JSON, which is set up as a cache: `maxmemory` set and `maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru`. Traffic grows and memory fills. What happens to the sessions?
hint: Web Servers and Caching, lesson 8; Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 7.

choices.text: New sign-ins fail with `OOM command not allowed`, while the sessions already there are kept.
choices.why: That is `noeviction`; under `allkeys-lru` every write succeeds and older keys make the room.

choices.text: They are safe, since only keys without a lifetime are evicted and every session carries one.
choices.why: `allkeys` means any key; it is the `volatile` policies that look only at keys with a lifetime, and they would pick the sessions.

choices.text: Evicted sessions are written to `dump.rdb` first, and come back after the next restart.
choices.why: Eviction deletes; a snapshot holds only what was in memory when it was taken.

choices.text: Idle sessions are evicted like any cached book, and those visitors are signed out early.
choices.why: Right. A cache may forget and a session table may not: give each one a Redis of its own.

prompt: In 2018, open Memcached servers flooded third parties over UDP with replies many thousands of times the size of the small forged requests that caused them. Why does the same trick not work against a Memcached that speaks only TCP?
hint: Web Servers and Caching, lesson 9; Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 2.

choices.text: TCP numbers its bytes, so Memcached can tell that a forged request's bytes are out of order.
choices.why: Numbering puts a stream back in order; it says nothing about who sent it.

choices.text: Before any data, TCP answers a SYN with a SYN-ACK, which goes to the forged address; the request never follows.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: TCP slows down when it sees loss, so a reply that large is throttled before it can do harm.
choices.why: Slowing down shares a congested link; it does not stop a large answer reaching whoever the request named.

choices.text: Over TCP, Memcached refuses any value larger than a megabyte, so the replies stay small.
choices.why: The one-megabyte limit is per value and holds however the request arrives; a megabyte is still huge beside a small request.

hint: Web Servers and Caching, lesson 10.

pairs.right: write-behind

pairs.left: Values read right after they change
pairs.right: write-through

pairs.left: Data written once and rarely read
pairs.right: write-around

pairs.right: cache-aside

prompt:
Your search handler reads `q` and `lang` from the query string, and `lang` never arrives, although people type in its box. The template has these two fields:

```html
<label for="q">Title or author</label>
<input id="q" name="q" type="search">
<label for="lang">Language</label>
<input id="lang">
```

What is wrong?
hint: HTML and CSS, lesson 3.

choices.text: The second label is joined by `for`, which makes its field one the browser shows and does not send.
choices.why: `for` joins a label to a field for its name and its click; it has nothing to do with what is sent.

choices.text: The second field has an `id` and no `name`, and a request is built only from `name=value` pairs.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A `get` form sends only its first field; the second would need `method="post"` to travel in the body.
choices.why: A GET form sends every named field, joined by `&`, in the query string.

choices.text: An input with no `type` is left out of the request until it is declared as `type="text"`.
choices.why: `text` is the default type; the field is skipped for having no name, not for its type.

prompt: A page lists a customer's reservations, each with a link `Cancel` that your server answers by deleting the reservation. One morning several reservations are gone, and nobody pressed anything. What do the two lessons say?
hint: HTML and CSS, lesson 3; Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 6.

choices.text: Links are acceptable here if the server answers `204 No Content`, which tells a crawler not to follow them.
choices.why: A status code arrives after the request has been carried out; by then the reservation is gone.

choices.text: Nothing in HTTP separates the two methods for this, so the cause is a bug in the delete query.
choices.why: GET is defined as safe, and that definition is exactly what lets anything fetch it freely.

choices.text: A `GET` is fine as long as the id is long and random, so that nobody can guess the address.
choices.why: The address is in the page itself, and whatever reads the page may fetch every link on it.

choices.text: A `GET` promises to change nothing, so anything may fetch it unasked; cancelling needs a `post` form.
choices.why: Right.

prompt: An old login page uses `<form action="login" method="get">`, so signing in sends `GET /login?user=ana&password=…` over HTTPS. Where is the password now written down? Choose all that apply.
hint: HTML and CSS, lesson 3; Web Servers and Caching, lesson 1.

choices.text: In the browser's history, with the rest of the address.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: In the server's access log, whose combined format records each request line.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: In plain text on the café's Wi-Fi, readable by anybody sharing it.
choices.why: HTTPS keeps the address out of other people's hands on the way; the copies that leak are the ones written down at each end.

choices.text: In the address the next site may receive as the page the visitor came from.
choices.why: Right.

prompt: The order page has `<input name="copies" type="number" min="1" max="5">`. Somebody skips the browser and sends your orders API `{"title": "Vidas Secas", "copies": -40}` with `Content-Type: application/json`. What should the API answer?
hint: HTML and CSS, lesson 3; APIs and Authentication, lesson 1.

choices.text: `422`, storing nothing: the JSON parses, and its content breaks a rule the server checks itself.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: `400`, because a body the page's form could never have produced is a malformed request.
choices.why: `400` is about the bytes: a body that is not JSON, or not an object. This one parses.

choices.text: `201`, with one copy stored: the form's `min` is the floor, so the server can move the value up to it.
choices.why: A value that fails a rule is refused and nothing is stored; the form's attributes never reached the server.

choices.text: `415`, since an order that bypassed the page did not arrive in the encoding the form uses.
choices.why: `415` is about the label, and this body is labelled `application/json`, which is what the API takes.

prompt: The order form has three checkboxes named `extra`. An order placed without touching any of them arrives as `GET /order?format=paperback&shop=centro&notes=`. How does your handler learn that nobody wanted gift wrap?
hint: HTML and CSS, lesson 3.

choices.text: From `notes=`, which the browser sends empty in place of the boxes nobody ticked.
choices.why: `notes` is the text area, sent empty because a text field always has a value; it says nothing about the boxes.

choices.text: It cannot, so the request should be refused for leaving out a field the form has.
choices.why: A missing `extra` is how the form says no; refusing it would refuse every order without extras.

choices.text: From the missing `extra`: an unchecked box sends nothing, so absence means no.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: From `extra=off`, which each unchecked box adds to the end of the query string.
choices.why: An unchecked checkbox sends nothing at all, neither `extra=` nor `extra=off`.

choices.text: Drop the pattern, which refuses *D'Ávila*, and question a 50 that no specification gave.

choices.text: Make the column `char(50)`, so every name is stored at one width and neither attribute is needed.
choices.why: `char(n)` pads with spaces, and comparisons and lengths then disagree about whether the spaces are there.

prompt: A recruiter has posted a junior back-end role on LinkedIn, and you want to send her a short message about it. When does lesson 7 say to send it?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 7.

choices.text: Before applying, so that she can say whether the CV is worth sending.
choices.why: A recruiter can do little with a message about a role you have not applied for, except ask you to apply.

choices.text: Instead of applying, with the CV attached, since a message gets read.
choices.why: The message goes after the application and carries no CV: they have it already.

choices.text: Every week until she answers, so the application stays near the top.
choices.why: Send it once; lesson 10 deals with what to do when there is no answer.

prompt: Run 2 of the lab's CI failed in all six cells: Ana had committed `tests/test_carriers.py`, and her laptop still shows `?? tests/data/carriers.csv`. Which of these puts the CSV into the commit the next run checks out?
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 5; Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 2.

choices.text: `git commit -am` with a message: `-a` stages the changes in the folder.
choices.why: `-a` only stages files git already tracks; a file marked `??` stays out of the commit.

choices.text: `git add` on the CSV, then a commit and a push: a new file needs its own add.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Push again as it is: the hook's clean checkout copies the files from the laptop.
choices.why: The checkout is `git archive` of the pushed commit, and only what was committed is in it.

choices.text: Add `tests/data/` to `.gitignore`, so that git stops reporting the file as untracked.
choices.why: Ignoring it hides the `??` and keeps the file out of every commit, which is the failure itself.

prompt: After tagging `v1.4.0`, Ana commits one more change and runs `ops/build.sh` without tagging again. `git describe --tags` prints `v1.4.0-1-g7c77050`. What does the build call the artifact?
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 7; Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 7.

choices.text: `shipquote-dev-7c77050`: no tag sits on that commit, so it is named by the commit.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: `shipquote-1.4.0`: the newest tag in the history that leads here is still `v1.4.0`.
choices.why: A tag does not move with new commits; `v1.4.0` names the commit before, and the build only uses a tag on HEAD itself.

choices.text: `shipquote-1.4.1`: a commit made after a release raises the patch number by one.
choices.why: Nothing raises a version on its own; the version is the tag on the commit, and here there is none.

choices.text: An error: `ops/build.sh` refuses to build a commit with no tag of its own.
choices.why: It builds, and names the result so that it cannot pass for a release.

prompt: Run 4 turned `main` red at commit `1247039`. Ana runs `git revert --no-edit HEAD`, pushes, and run 5 passes on `b33d78b`. What does `main`'s history hold now?
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 5; Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 4.

choices.text: `6b77129` at the top again: the revert moved `main` back to the commit before.
choices.why: That is what `git reset` does; a revert adds a commit and moves nothing back.

choices.text: `b33d78b` in the place of `1247039`, which the revert swapped for a corrected copy.
choices.why: A revert replaces nothing; swapping the last commit for a new one is what `--amend` does.

choices.text: `1247039` and, on top of it, `b33d78b`, a new commit that does the opposite.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: `1247039` alone, with its change undone inside it and no new commit made.
choices.why: A commit is never edited in place: its id covers its content, so any change is a new commit.

prompt: The lab's `post-receive` hook reported run 4 as failed, and the broken commit was on `main` all the same. On a hosting service, what would have kept it out?
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 5; Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 8.

choices.text: `set -e` at the top of the hook, so that its first failing cell rejects the push.
choices.why: The hook runs after git has accepted the push; nothing it does then can refuse it.

choices.text: A pull request into a protected `main` whose checks must pass before the merge.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Pushing with `-u`, so that git waits for the checks before it moves `origin/main`.
choices.why: `-u` only records which remote branch yours goes with; git itself knows nothing of checks.

choices.text: Nothing can: a Git server takes any push that moves a branch forward.
choices.why: Git does take it; the hosting service adds branch protection on top, which Git knows nothing about.

prompt: A release of the repository that publishes this course starts from a tag. Put the steps in order, from the developer's terminal to the new revision serving.
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 7; Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 7.
items: Push the annotated tag on its own, with `git push origin` and its name
`Tag` refuses a malformed tag, one lower than the last release, or one off `main`
`Checks` runs the whole CI workflow, called rather than copied
`Publish` builds, asks the binary its version and creates the release
`Deploy` pushes the images and moves the service to the new revision
trap: Building first looks quicker, but each job needs the one before: the tag is judged before anything runs, and nothing is built from a commit the checks have not passed. A plain `git push` would not even start it, because it sends no tags.

prompt: Ana runs `git push -u origin try-new-rounding` against the lab's remote, and the hook answers `ci: try-new-rounding is not main, nothing to run`. What happened?
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 5; Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 7.

choices.text: The branch now exists on the remote, and no test ran on it.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The push was refused, because the hook turns away pushes to other branches.
choices.why: The hook decides whether to run tests, not whether to accept; `* [new branch]` shows the branch was received.

choices.text: The tests ran and passed, which is why the hook printed so little.
choices.why: A passing run still prints a line per cell and `run N passed`; this one ran nothing.

choices.text: The branch was merged into `main` first, so that the hook could test it.
choices.why: Nothing merges on a push; the branch arrived as it was, beside `main`.

prompt: On a branch nobody has pushed, Ana committed `deploy/production.env` with the carrier token, then removed it in the next commit. Bruno says that since the branch never left her laptop, `git reset --hard HEAD~2` settles it. What do the two courses say to do?
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 10; Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 9.

choices.text: Leave it: the second commit already took the token out of the history.
choices.why: `git show HEAD~1:deploy/production.env` still prints it; deleting a file does not change the commit that added it.

choices.text: The reset settles it: a commit kept on her own laptop has reached no other copy.
choices.why: Both courses treat a committed secret as public from that moment; the reset only stops it spreading.

choices.text: Run `git filter-repo` over the history and replace each clone before anything else.
choices.why: That is the route for commits already pushed, and even then it comes after revoking the token.

choices.text: Rotate the token first; after that, the reset is a fine way to drop both commits.
choices.why: Right.

prompt: Match each thing that went wrong to the quickest way back the two courses give for it.

prompt: A team works trunk based: the half-built delivery estimate is merged into `main` every day behind `delivery_estimate`, which production now has at 10%. Its CI runs the suite with every flag off. What does that leave untested?
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 9; Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 10.

choices.text: Little that matters: below 100% most customers have it off, so off is the state to test.
choices.why: At 10% both paths run in production; a suite that only knows every flag off tests a program nobody runs.

choices.text: The merging: with a flag, trunk-based work should stay on its branch until it is done.
choices.why: Merging unfinished work behind a flag is the point of trunk based; the gap is in the tests, not the branch.

choices.text: The flags file, which the program reads once at start-up and then keeps in memory.
choices.why: `flags.load()` reads the file on every request; that is how 10% became 50% with no restart.

choices.text: The path the 10% of customers take: a flag mid-rollout has to be tested in both of its states.
choices.why: Right.

prompt: At 15:00 on a later day, Ana runs `git log --oneline --since="2026-09-17"` on the bakery's week. `6555c9b` and `eadf998` are listed, but `31a6298 Add cheese rolls`, committed at 10:15 on the 17th, is not. Why?
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 3.

choices.text: `--since` keeps what came after the day named, so the 17th itself is left out.
choices.why: The day is not excluded as such; with `00:00` written after the date, the same command lists `31a6298`.

choices.text: The commit's date is in `-0300`, and `--since` compares it in UTC, three hours later.
choices.why: The zone is part of the stored date and is taken into account; the missing piece is the hour.

choices.text: A date with no time means that day at the current time of day, here 15:00.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The log filled the first screen and waited, so the older commit sits further down.
choices.why: `git log` does page long output, but three lines fit on any screen; nothing is waiting below.

prompt: Ana is on `main` with a clean working tree, and Bruno has just pushed a new commit to `origin`. Which of these commands change files in her working tree? Choose all that apply.

choices.why: It copies his commit and moves `origin/main`; her own `main` and her files stay as they were.

choices.text: `git pull`, which here fast-forwards `main`
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: `git branch menu-prices`, to start new work
choices.why: It writes a name for the current commit and copies nothing; she is still on `main`.

choices.text: `git switch experiment`, whose `index.html` differs
choices.why: Right.

prompt: Mutation testing left a survivor in `store.py`: `ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC` changed to `ORDER BY created_at DESC`. Which new test would kill it?
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 4.

choices.text: Two quotes with the same `created_at`, and `recent(2)` expected to list the newer id first.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A quote saved with negative cents, and the database expected to refuse it.
choices.why: That kills the other survivor, the loosened `CHECK (cents >= 0)`; it never reaches the ordering.

choices.text: Any test that raises the coverage of `store.py`, since a survivor marks a line nobody ran.
choices.why: `store.py` is already at 100%: the line ran, and what is missing is an assertion that tells the orders apart.

choices.text: Ten quotes from the factory, and `recent(10)` expected to list the ten, newest first.
choices.why: The factory gives every quote its own `created_at`, so the tie-break on `id` is never needed.

prompt: On GitHub Actions, a suite has one failing test and coverage stands at 81%. Which of these `run:` steps would still show green? Choose all that apply.
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lessons 4 and 5.

choices.text: No `shell:` line, running `python -m pytest -q | tee run.log`
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: `shell: bash`, running `python -m pytest -q | tee run.log`
choices.why: Naming the shell gives `-eo pipefail`, so pytest's failure fails the pipe and the step.

choices.text: No `shell:` line, running `coverage report --fail-under=85 | tail -1`
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: No `shell:` line, running `python -m pytest -q` on its own
choices.why: `bash -e` stops on pytest's non-zero status; it is the pipe that hides one.

prompt: A script reads a setting from a file a colleague wrote in a Windows editor: `mode=$(cat mode.txt)`. `echo "$mode"` prints `prod`, and yet `[ "$mode" = prod ]` is false every time it runs. What is going on?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 1.

choices.text: `$( )` keeps the file's final newline, so the value is really `prod` followed by a line break.
choices.why: `$( )` strips trailing newlines; the `\n` is gone, and the character before it is not.

choices.text: The lines end in `\r\n`, so the value is `prod` and a carriage return, which `cat -A` shows as `^M`.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Inside `[ ]`, `=` compares numbers, so two words do not compare as equal; a comparison of strings needs `==` there.
choices.why: `=` is the string comparison in `[ ]`; the letter operators, `-eq` and the rest, are for numbers.

choices.text: `mode` was never exported, so the `[` command receives an empty value to compare.
choices.why: `[` is handed the value already expanded, as an argument; `export` only matters to a child reading its environment.

prompt: Your service's image is `FROM alpine:3.22`, and the build copies in a monitoring agent downloaded as a prebuilt Linux x86_64 binary. The file is there and executable, but it refuses to start, with an error about a missing shared library. The same binary runs on your Ubuntu laptop. What is wrong, and what do the two lessons suggest?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 2; Docker and Containers, lesson 13.

choices.text: Alpine's `/bin/sh` is busybox `ash`, not bash, so it has to be added with `apk add --no-cache bash`.
choices.why: That is what breaks a `#!/bin/bash` script. A compiled program needs no shell, and the library it misses is the C library.

choices.text: It was built for another processor, and rebuilding the image for `arm64` will let it start.
choices.why: It runs on an x86_64 laptop, so the architecture matches; what differs between the two machines is the C library.

choices.text: Busybox lacks the GNU flags the agent calls `ls` and `grep` with, so install the GNU tools beside it.
choices.why: A missing flag fails later, on that flag. A missing shared library is the program refused before it runs at all.

choices.text: It was linked against glibc and Alpine ships musl; build on a Debian `-slim` base, which has glibc.
choices.why: Right.

prompt: An image builds a tool into `/app/bin` during `docker build`. To try a code change, a teammate runs it with `-v "$PWD":/app`, and inside the container `/app/bin` is not there. Run without the `-v`, it is. What happened to it?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 3; Docker and Containers, lesson 8.

choices.text: The host directory lies over `/app` and covers what the image put there, which is untouched.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The mount copied the host directory into the image and replaced `/app/bin` there for good, layer and all.
choices.why: Nothing in the image changes. Without the mount the files are back, the way `oops.txt` came back after `umount`.

choices.text: A bind mount is read-only by default, so the container does not see what it did not write itself.
choices.why: Read-only is `:ro`, added on purpose, and it is about writing; it does not decide what is visible.

choices.text: `docker run` discards the build layer holding `/app/bin` whenever a volume is passed to it at start.
choices.why: No layer is thrown away; the mount sits on top of the directory and the layer is still underneath it.

prompt: On a new server you ran `sudo usermod -aG docker ana`. In the same terminal, `getent group docker` prints `docker:x:996:ana`, yet `docker ps` answers `permission denied while trying to connect to the docker API at unix:///var/run/docker.sock`. What do you do?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 4; Docker and Containers, lesson 5.

choices.text: Run `usermod -G docker ana` instead, since `-a` only appends to the file and grants nothing yet.
choices.why: `-G` without `-a` replaces every other supplementary group, which is how people lose `sudo`; the change is already written.

choices.text: Run `sudo chmod 666 /var/run/docker.sock`, so the socket stops checking the group of whoever connects.
choices.why: That hands every account on the machine what the docker group amounts to, and the group amounts to root.

choices.text: Log out and in again: a shell keeps the groups it began with, and `id -nG` then shows `docker`.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Start the engine with `sudo systemctl start docker`, because the daemon is not running yet.
choices.why: A stopped engine answers `failed to connect to the docker API`; `permission denied` means it is up and refused you.

prompt: A colleague hand-wrote a unit file for a nightly importer. Match each line in it to what systemd actually does with it, by lesson 5.
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 5.

pairs.left: `Descriptoin=Nightly importer`
pairs.right: dropped with a warning nobody sees unless `systemd-analyze verify` is run

pairs.left: `ExecStart=/usr/bin/importer > /var/log/importer.log`
pairs.right: the `>` and the path reach the program as two more arguments

pairs.left: `Type=forking`, for a program that stays in the foreground
pairs.right: the start hangs, then times out, with nothing actually broken

pairs.left: `After=network.target`
pairs.right: it starts once the network is configured, which is not when it is reachable

right_distractors: the whole unit is refused and never loads

prompt: A service's Dockerfile ends with `CMD ./start.sh`, in shell form, and the script starts the server on its last line. Every `docker stop` takes ten seconds, the container then shows `Exited (137)`, and the server's log never has its shutdown message. What explains all three?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 6; Docker and Containers, lesson 11.

choices.text: The server catches `TERM` and is still flushing when the ten seconds run out, so a longer stop timeout would turn 137 into 0.
choices.why: With no shutdown line in the log the server never received the signal at all, and waiting longer only delays the `KILL`.

choices.text: `TERM` reaches a shell that does not pass it on; after the wait comes `KILL`, 128 + 9. Use exec form and `exec` the server.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: 137 is the out-of-memory killer at work, so the container needs a higher memory limit before it can stop any faster.
choices.why: 137 is any `KILL`. A memory kill is recorded as `OOMKilled=true`; this one is `docker stop`'s own `KILL` after its wait.

choices.text: `docker stop` sends `KILL` straight away, and the ten seconds are the engine first saving the container's layer.
choices.why: It sends the polite signal first and waits ten seconds before the `KILL`; the stopped container keeps its layer regardless.

prompt: You are writing the `RUN` instruction that installs `ca-certificates` in a Dockerfile built on Debian. Which of these belong in it, by the two lessons? Choose all that apply.
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 7; Docker and Containers, lesson 14.

choices.text: `apt-get` rather than `apt`, whose output its authors may change
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: `rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*` as a separate `RUN`, at the end of the file
choices.why: A file deleted in a later layer is still in the earlier one; the cleanup has to be in the same `RUN`.

choices.text: `--no-install-recommends`, so only what `Depends` lists arrives
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: `dpkg -i` on a `.deb` fetched first, so no dependency resolution runs
choices.why: `dpkg` resolves nothing: a missing dependency leaves the package unpacked and unconfigured, `iU`.

prompt: Your Nginx access log is in the combined format, with lines like `127.0.0.1 - - [07/Oct/2026:00:11:23 -0300] "GET /css/site.css HTTP/1.0" 200 237 "-" "ApacheBench/2.3"`. To count client errors, a teammate runs `grep -c ' 4[0-9][0-9] ' access.log`, which reports more than `awk '$9 >= 400 && $9 < 500' access.log | wc -l`. Which count do you trust?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 8; Web Servers and Caching, lesson 1.

choices.text: grep's: awk splits on spaces, so it loses the lines whose user agent has a space inside it.
choices.why: The user agent comes after field nine. A free-text field only moves the fields after it, so `$9` is the status on every line.

choices.text: grep's: awk reads each field as text, so a status such as `404` is not `>= 400` to it.
choices.why: `$9 >= 400` is arithmetic on a field, which is the thing `grep` cannot do.

choices.text: awk's: the status is field nine, and the pattern also matches a `200` whose size, in field ten, happens to be 410.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: awk's: `grep -c` counts each match on a line, so a line holding two such numbers is counted twice.
choices.why: `grep -c` counts matching lines, not matches; a line is counted once however many times it matches.

prompt: A CI step runs a script that begins `set -euo pipefail`, defines `check() { ./migrate --dry-run; echo "migrations checked"; }` and then runs `if check; then ./deploy.sh; fi`. `./migrate` fails and prints an error, the deploy happens anyway, and the job is green. Why did nothing stop?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 9; Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 5.

choices.text: `-e` is suspended for the whole of a function called as a condition, so `check` ran on and returned the `echo`'s 0.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The CI reads the step's output for errors, and `migrations checked` was the last line it saw printed there.
choices.why: A CI decides on the exit status alone; it never reads the output, so the words printed cannot turn a step green or red.

choices.text: With `pipefail` set, `-e` stops applying, and `pipefail` itself looks at pipelines and nothing else.
choices.why: The two are independent: `pipefail` changes what a pipeline reports, and `-e` still applies everywhere it applies.

choices.text: `-e` does not reach inside a function, so a failure inside `check` is ignored wherever it is called from.
choices.why: Called as a plain command, a failing line inside a function does stop the script; the suspension comes from the `if`.

prompt: Renaming Arena Sul in lesson 5's MongoDB rewrote 33 show documents, because each show embeds its venue's name. A colleague concludes that `order_lines.unit_price` in the SQL shop is the same mistake, a copy of `products.price`, and proposes dropping it. By lesson 2's test, what is wrong with that?
hint: Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 2; Scale and Observability, lesson 5.

choices.text: Nothing: both repeat a value that is held in another table, and third normal form removes every repeated value.
choices.why: 3NF removes a repeated fact that can disagree with itself; it says nothing against two different facts that once had the same value.

choices.text: A renamed venue should reach every show, so it is a copy; the price paid must not move, so it is a snapshot.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The price is safe because `numeric` is exact, which a string embedded in a document is not.
choices.why: The type has nothing to do with it; the test is whether the value should change when its source does.

choices.text: It counts 1 April too, because `BETWEEN` includes its upper bound and the day after it.
choices.why: The upper bound is `2026-03-31 00:00:00`, and nothing in April is reached.

prompt: Suppose each ticket stores the idempotency key of its sale, and payments exports its charges carrying the same key. After a day of timeouts you want one query listing both the charges with no ticket and the tickets with no charge. Which shape does it?

choices.text: `tickets t JOIN charges c ON c.key = t.key`, and then read the rows where one side is null
choices.why: An inner join keeps only the pairs; the rows with no partner are exactly the ones it drops.

choices.text: `tickets t LEFT JOIN charges c ON c.key = t.key`, keeping only the rows where `c.key IS NULL`
choices.why: That finds the tickets with no charge and never sees a charge with no ticket.

choices.text: `SELECT * FROM charges WHERE key NOT IN (SELECT key FROM tickets)`
choices.why: One direction only, and a single null key in `tickets` makes it return nothing at all.

prompt: Lesson 7's SLI is good events over all events. Somebody computes it from a table of request logs with `SELECT count(CASE WHEN ms <= 250 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)::numeric / count(*) FROM request_log`, and it says 1 even on the day sales took seconds. Why?
hint: Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 6; Scale and Observability, lesson 7.

choices.text: The `::numeric` comes too late, so the division is done on two integers and rounds to 1.
choices.why: The cast applies to the first count before the division, so the result is a decimal; the numerator is simply every row.

choices.text: `ms <= 250` is unknown for the slow rows, and the `CASE` treats an unknown condition as if it were true.
choices.why: Unknown appears only where `ms` is null; a slow request has a value, and for it the comparison is false.

choices.text: `count` counts the zeros too, since 0 is not null, so the top is every row.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: `count(*)` skips the rows whose `CASE` gave 0, so both sides shrink together.
choices.why: `count(*)` counts rows and has no argument to skip on; it is the `count(CASE …)` that should have skipped and did not.

prompt: The box office's monthly sales report reads a materialised view that a nightly job refreshes, and scale lesson 11 says a degraded answer should say how old it is. One night the refresh fails. What does SQL lesson 7 suggest so that every reader can tell?

choices.text: Store `now() AS refreshed_at` in it, which every report then prints.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Refresh it `CONCURRENTLY`, so readers keep working while the new contents are being built.
choices.why: That keeps the view readable during a refresh; it says nothing on the night the refresh never happened.

choices.text: Create it `WITH NO DATA`, so that a failed refresh becomes an error instead of old rows.
choices.why: Only a view never filled is an error; one filled last week keeps answering with last week.

choices.text: Replace it with a plain view, which the database caches for you and refreshes on its own schedule.
choices.why: A plain view stores no rows; it reruns the query on every read, which is the cost the materialised one was avoiding.

prompt: On the primary, `pg_stat_user_indexes` shows an index on `orders (placed_at)` with `idx_scan` at 0 and a size of several hundred megabytes. Reports and dashboards are sent to a read replica, as scale lesson 2 recommends. What should you do before dropping it?

choices.why: The primary's counter only sees the primary's queries, and the reports run somewhere else.

choices.text: Read the counter on the replica as well: each server counts only the scans that were made on it.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Check that it does not back a `UNIQUE` constraint, and drop it if it does not.
choices.why: That is the check for a unique index, which this one is not; and the counter it trusts is the wrong server's.

choices.text: Drop it on the primary only, so that the replica can keep its own copy of the index for the reports.
choices.why: A replica applies the primary's log and ends up the same database a moment later; an index dropped there is dropped on the replica.

What is it, and what fixes it?
hint: Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 11; Scale and Observability, lesson 8.

choices.text: Too many spans: tail-sample the page so that only the slow traces keep their query spans.
choices.why: Sampling changes what is recorded, not what runs; the fifty queries still reach the database.

choices.text: A missing index on `orders.customer_id`: add it, and each of the fifty queries gets faster.
choices.why: Each one already takes a millisecond; the cost is the count of round trips, and an index does not change the count.

choices.text: A slow database: give it more CPU, so that fifty round trips fit in the time of a few.
choices.why: The N+1 is not fixed by a bigger server: what it costs is round trips, not work.

choices.text: An N+1: fetch the orders of all fifty customers at once, in one query, with `= ANY(…)`.
choices.why: Right.

prompt: The first version of the box office ran on SQLite in WAL mode and was fast. For the on-sale the team wants scale lesson 1's horizontal scaling: three copies of the program, on three machines, behind nginx. What does SQL lesson 12 say?

choices.text: It works once WAL is on, because WAL lets each copy write at the same time.
choices.why: WAL lets readers and the single writer proceed together; there is still one writer.

choices.text: It works if the file is put on a network filesystem that all three machines mount.
choices.why: SQLite's locking depends on file locks that network filesystems implement unreliably, and it is not supported.

choices.text: It is out: the file must be on the machine the code runs on.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: It works with a busy timeout, which turns each `database is locked` into a short queue.
choices.why: A busy timeout queues the writers of one machine; it does not let three machines share one file.

prompt: On a corporate Oracle system you propose scale lesson 2's arrangement: a replica that takes the reports off the primary. Why does such a system often have none?

choices.text: A second server is another licence, and reading a standby while it applies is a separately priced option.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Oracle has no replication: a standby can only be rebuilt from last night's backup.
choices.why: Data Guard keeps a standby current from the redo stream; reading from it is what costs extra.

choices.text: Read consistency from undo makes a replica unnecessary, since a long report there never blocks a writer.
choices.why: Readers do not block writers, and the reports still compete for the same machine; what rules the replica out is the bill.

choices.text: Replicas need the Diagnostics Pack to report their lag, and few systems license it.
choices.why: The Diagnostics Pack is AWR and ASH, the performance history; it has nothing to do with whether a standby exists.

choices.text: The sales deadlock on the show's row, and after a second PostgreSQL cancels one of them to break the cycle.

choices.text: Two of them see the same count and store the same result, so an increment vanishes: the lost update.
choices.why: Right.

prompt: After the backfill, `ALTER TABLE tickets ALTER COLUMN gate SET NOT NULL` found the valid `CHECK (gate IS NOT NULL)` and skipped its scan, yet it took 1.1 seconds. Why that long, and why about one second?

choices.why: A detected deadlock rolls one side back with an error; the change succeeded, and the sales never held its lock.

choices.text: Autovacuum's conflicting lock, which PostgreSQL cancels after `deadlock_timeout`, one second.
choices.why: Right.

prompt: `pg_stat_statements` puts the lookup by email at a mean of 0.0 ms over 400 calls, while the program making the calls times each one at a few milliseconds. Scale lesson 7 met the same gap: a 95th percentile for reads of 20 ms from the box office's histogram and 30 ms from `load.py`. What explains both?
hint: Scale and Observability, lesson 7; Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 10.

choices.text: A time measured inside a service is a lower bound: the caller's clock also holds the network and the wait to be served.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Each inside number is interpolated within a bucket, and interpolation always comes out low.
choices.why: Interpolation is how a percentile comes out of buckets; it can land either side, and the mean in `pg_stat_statements` is not built that way.

choices.text: One side of each pair is wrong, since two measurements of one thing that disagree mean broken instrumentation.
choices.why: Agreement is the check when both measure the same span; these measure different spans, and both are right.

choices.text: The outside clock counts a queue that a closed-loop generator builds on purpose.
choices.why: A closed loop waits for each answer before sending the next; it builds no queue of its own requests.

choices.text: Each sale now holds the show's row lock through the call to payments as well as `sign()`, so that row's queue grows.

choices.text: Page reads of that show now wait behind the lock for as long as each charge takes.

choices.text: Jitter only matters when callers retry at the same instant, and the checkout's backoff had already spread its retries.
choices.why: Backoff without jitter moves the spike rather than spreading it; that is why jitter exists.

choices.text: Full jitter can draw a wait of zero, so some retries come straight back and restart the storm by themselves.
choices.why: A few immediate retries are part of the spread; the storm needs far more calls than that.

choices.text: It spreads retries in time without making fewer of them: every request still makes up to four calls.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Jitter belongs in the stock service, which decides when to answer, not in the client.
choices.why: Jitter is the caller's random wait before retrying; the service has nothing to randomise.

prompt: The shop of lesson 12 runs with no bound on its orders queue (`QUEUE` unset), and its one worker handles ten orders a second. A burst of 300 orders arrives all at once and every one is answered `202 Accepted`. About how many seconds does the last of them wait before it is handled?
hint: Systems Architecture, lesson 12.

prompt: In lesson 13's design each order is its own event stream, guarded by `UNIQUE (stream, version)`. Two customers, each in their own order, add the last bag of coffee and pay at the same moment. What stops the shop from selling two bags it does not have?
hint: Systems Architecture, lesson 13.

choices.text: Nothing in the order streams: no command loads two streams, so the rule needs a stock stream every order appends to, or a saga.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The unique constraint, since both commands try to append the same version number to the one events table, and the later is refused.
choices.why: The constraint is per stream; two different orders each writing their own version 2 never collide.

choices.text: The projection, which refuses an `OrderPaid` that would take `units_sold` past the stock.
choices.why: A projection builds read models after the fact; it does not refuse events.

choices.text: Optimistic concurrency, which reloads the second order and finds the coffee already sold.
choices.why: Reloading an order replays that order's events only; another customer's sale is not in them.

prompt: Quitanda's orchestrated checkout reserves the coffee, charges the card, schedules the delivery and confirms the reservation as sold. The team now wants it to send an "order confirmed" e-mail too. Where does lesson 14 put that step?
hint: Systems Architecture, lesson 14.

choices.text: First, so the customer hears at once, with a correction e-mail as its compensation if a later step fails.
choices.why: An e-mail sent cannot be taken back; a second one is another fact, not an undo.

choices.text: Between the reservation and the charge, because the reservation already guarantees that the coffee is there.
choices.why: The charge and the delivery can still fail after it, and the e-mail would then be false.

choices.text: Anywhere in the list, as long as the step is idempotent, since a retried e-mail then goes out only once.
choices.why: Idempotency stops a duplicate; it does not undo an e-mail that a later failure makes untrue.

choices.text: After the delivery is scheduled, the pivot, because an e-mail cannot be compensated and the saga only goes forward from there.
choices.why: Right.

prompt: Quitanda is moving its stock data out of the monolith and into the new stock service behind the strangler facade. Put the steps in the order lesson 15 gives them.
hint: Systems Architecture, lesson 15.
items: Make the stock module the only way in to its tables, inside the monolith
Give the new service a copy, fed by change data capture or an outbox
Send the reads to the new service through the facade, a share at a time
Move the writes, so the new service becomes the owner
Stop the copying and drop the old tables
trap: Moving the writes early feels like the real migration, but the owner should change only after the reads have shown the copy agrees, and the old tables go last, once nothing reads them.

prompt: `pg_stat_statements` shows the items query of Quitanda's order history called once per order, a multiple of the orders query. A teammate fixes it by marking the order's items as always loaded eagerly, on the model class. What do the two lessons say about that fix?
hint: Systems Architecture, lesson 16; Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 11.

choices.text: It is the recommended fix, because eager loading marked on the class removes every N+1 in the whole application at once.
choices.why: It removes this N+1 and adds a cost to every other screen that loads an order.

choices.text: This N+1 goes, but every screen that loads an order now fetches its items too; the instruction belongs at the loop.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: It cannot work, because eager loading is a join, and a join on a to-many relationship returns the wrong rows for each order.
choices.why: A join on a to-many relationship repeats the parent; the rows are correct, only larger.

choices.text: It moves the problem into the database, which now runs the same N+1 as a stored procedure.
choices.why: Eager loading sends one query per level, or a join; nothing loops inside the database.

prompt: Quitanda's index analyses names with `portuguese_folded`: `lowercase`, `asciifolding` and the Brazilian stemmer. Without `--fuzzy`, which of these words, typed alone into the search box, become a term that `Café torrado em grãos` was stored with? Choose all that apply.
hint: Systems Architecture, lesson 17.

choices.text: `cafe`
choices.why: Folded and stemmed, it is `caf`, the same term as `Café`.

choices.text: `torado`
choices.why: One letter short; it is not a term in the index, and only `--fuzzy` reaches `torr` from it.

choices.text: `torrada`
choices.why: The stemmer cuts `torrado`, `torrada` and `torrados` to `torr`.

choices.text: `tostado`
choices.why: A different word with a different stem, found in the mate tea's name and not in this one.

prompt: Quitanda's order page opens a Server-Sent Events stream through Nginx, whose `/api/` location sets `proxy_read_timeout 3s`. An order changes a few times an hour. What happens to the stream, and what do the two lessons suggest?
hint: Systems Architecture, lesson 18; Web Servers and Caching, lesson 2.

choices.text: Nginx cuts it after three silent seconds; give it a block of its own with a longer timeout, or write something sooner.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Nothing, because `proxy_read_timeout` only limits how long the shop takes to start answering, and the stream started at once.
choices.why: It is the gap between two reads of the response, and an idle stream has long gaps.

choices.text: Nginx closes it after three seconds whatever is sent, because the timeout caps the whole request.
choices.why: None of Nginx's timeouts caps the total; a response that trickles a byte in time never times out.

choices.text: The stream survives, because Nginx never applies its read timeout to a response of type `text/event-stream`.
choices.why: Nginx treats the stream like any other response from the shop.
